title: J.P. Morgan raises $1.1bn as net lease platform takes shape - Alternatives Watch
content: Chad Tredway, J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s global head of real estate and head of Real Estate Americas (Photo credit: J.P. Morgan) J.P. Morgan Asset Management has closed its inaugural net lease fund with $1.1 billion in commitments, giving the firm plenty of capital to deploy into a strategy it began building through an acquisition nearly three years ago. J.P. Morgan Net Lease Real Estate Fund II exceeded its initial $500 million target, with commitments from investors in the U.S., Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East. More than half of the investors are new to J.P. Morgan Asset Management Real Estate Americas. Los Angeles County Employees Retirement Association committed $200 million to the fund. The U.S.-focused vehicle will acquire single-tenant properties under long-term, triple-net leases. The strategy also targets sale-leaseback transactions, which allow companies to raise capital from owned real estate while remaining tenants of the properties. “Net lease will continue to be a focus for J.P. Morgan Asset Management, and this is just the beginning of providing our clients with greater access to this segment of the real estate market,” said Chad Tredway, the firm’s global head of real estate. Tredway returned to J.P. Morgan in December 2023 when the firm acquired Trio, the investment manager he founded after leaving the bank in 2021. Tredway had spent 13 years at J.P. Morgan before forming Trio, including as head of Real Estate Banking in the Commercial Bank division. In that role, he led a team of 250 and oversaw more than $20 billion in real estate loans. He also played a role in establishing a U.S. multifamily lending portfolio with more than $80 billion in assets. Trio, which focused on institutional sale-leaseback investments, had grown to $250 million in assets by the time J.P. Morgan brought it into the firm. Upon his return, Tredway was named head of J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s Real Estate Americas, then a $74 billion equity and debt platform. His initial mandate included integrating Trio and expanding the portfolio team, making the acquisition the starting point for a broader net lease push rather than a stand-alone transaction. In the fall of 2024, J.P. Morgan Asset Management hired Justin Heller to head the net lease strategy, reporting to Tredway. Heller came from TPG Angelo Gordon, where he worked on sourcing, underwriting, and originating net lease transactions and had led the sale of about $5 billion in assets. By May 2025, Tredway’s remit had widened. J.P. Morgan named him head of its $79 billion global real estate business, placing operations in the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific under his leadership. David Chen, CIO and head of Real Estate APAC, and Michael Ramm, CIO and head of Real Estate Europe, began reporting to him, while Tredway retained oversight of Real Estate Americas. J.P. Morgan Asset Management now reports $80 billion in global real estate assets under management and $4.6 trillion in firmwide assets under management as of June 30. Net Lease Real Estate Fund II is positioned to benefit from net lease transaction volume that reached $13.8 billion in the second quarter, up 24.1% from a year earlier and the highest second-quarter total since 2022, according to data released by Newmark this week. Industrial properties accounted for more than 60% of U.S. net lease sales volume after transaction volume in the sector rose 33.7% from a year earlier. Retail volume increased 30.4%, while the number of retail transactions was roughly unchanged. Office moved in the other direction, with volume down 13.1% and cap rates reaching 8%. The industrial concentration overlaps with the Net Lease Real Estate Fund II mandate. J.P. Morgan Asset Management said it is targeting properties tied to supply chains, manufacturing, and logistics, and executives pointed to manufacturing growth, onshoring, and demand for sale-leaseback capital as drivers of activity in the sector. Other major asset managers have been busy adding to their own net lease businesses. Goldman Sachs agreed in August to acquire LCN Capital Partners, which manages about $3 billion and invests in sale-leaseback, build-to-suit, and triple-net-lease real estate in North America and Europe. The acquisition will add LCN’s strategy to Goldman’s private real estate platform. Blue Owl Capital, meanwhile, closed its first European net lease fund in August with €1.6 billion, or $1.84 billion, in commitments. The fund exceeded its €1 billion target and €1.5 billion hard cap. Blue Owl entered the net lease business through its 2021 acquisition of Oak Street Real Estate Capital and has since extended the strategy into Europe. Apollo also moved into a portfolio of net lease properties this year through a $1 billion investment for a 49% stake in a joint venture with Realty Income. The venture was set to hold about 500 single-tenant retail properties across the U.S., generating $140 million in annualized base rent. Back at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, the firm said Net Lease Real Estate Fund II already has an acquisition pipeline across property types and logistics markets and is ready to leverage J.P. Morgan’s decades of corporate and banking relationships to expand a business likely to play a growing role in its global real estate operation. The Federal Reserve's Sept. 15-16 policy meeting has become unusually consequential for investors as inflation remains above the central bank's 2% target, the labor market shows signs of renewed strength and geopolitical tensions push crude oil sharply higher. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that nonfarm payroll employment increased by 162,000 in August, well above the 31,000 average monthly gain over the prior 12 months, while the unemployment rate held at 4.1%. The stronger-than-expected employment report has increased expectations for a potential rate hike, with futures markets assigning roughly a 59% probability to a 25-basis-point increase, according to Reuters. Inflation remains another key constraint. July CPI increased 3.4% year over year, while core CPI rose 2.5%, according to the BLS. The August PPI and CPI reports are scheduled for Sept. 10 and Sept. 11, respectively, immediately before the Fed meeting. Against this backdrop, JPMorgan Chase JPM, EOG Resources EOG and Bloom Energy BE offer exposure to three distinct forces shaping the market ahead of the Fed meeting — interest rates, elevated crude prices and structural electricity demand from AI infrastructure. Let's delve deeper. The Fed's policy calculus has become more difficult as the energy market has deteriorated. Brent crude briefly moved above $100 per barrel on Sept. 9 for the first time since July 24 (Reuters), after escalating U.S.-Iran tensions and attacks by Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi energy facilities heightened concerns about supply disruptions. The oil shock could complicate the inflation outlook by lifting energy costs while simultaneously weighing on household purchasing power and economic growth. The New York Fed's August Survey of Consumer Expectations showed one-year inflation expectations holding at 3.6%, while the perceived probability of higher unemployment over the next year rose to 44.4%, its highest level since April 2020. Treasury yields are also responding to the changing inflation and policy outlook, with the 10-year yield approaching 4.8%-5%. Higher yields raise corporate borrowing costs and increase the discount rate applied to future earnings, potentially pressuring equity valuations. Its low-cost operating model and diversified oil, natural gas liquids and natural-gas portfolio also provide some insulation against commodity-cycle volatility. title: JPMorgan Gains as Its European Hiring Offensive Reaches Greece - TradingView
content: JPMorgan Chase JPM, the largest U.S. bank by assets, climbed approximately 0.5% to $355.01 Wednesday as it pushed its corporate-banking franchise into Greece. The new operation will bring lending, financing, hedging and investment-banking services to large and midsized Greek companies. The bank has expanded staffing across its Europe, Middle East and Africa global corporate bank by roughly 25% over the past two years. Greece gives JPMorgan another gateway for connecting local companies with its global payments and capital-markets machinery. Management did not disclose a revenue target or planned headcount for the country. JPMorgan generated $58 billion in managed second-quarter revenue and $21.2 billion in net income, while overseeing approximately $5 trillion in assets. Greece is too small to transform those numbers overnight, but it can strengthen cross-border relationships without forcing the bank to recreate its product engine. The picture adds a valuation warning: the $355.01 share price sits 12.24% above the $316.30 GF Value estimate, suggesting investors already pay a premium for JPMorgan's scale and execution. title: JP Morgan boss meets Burnham and Healey amid fears of bank tax raid - The Telegraph
content: Jamie Dimon lobbies Chancellor to resist pressure to target lenders in effort to fill Budget shortfall Tom Saunders is The Telegraph's Financial Correspondent. He was named one of MHP's 30 To Watch young journalists and won the European Parliament's Daphne Caruana Galizia prize for journalism. He previously worked as a business reporter at The Times. Email him at tom.saunders@telegraph.co.uk or find him on X @tomjs Tom Saunders is The Telegraph's Financial Correspondent. He was named one of MHP's 30 To Watch young journalists and won the European Parliament's Daphne Caruana Galizia prize for journalism. He previously worked as a business reporter at The Times. Email him at tom.saunders@telegraph.co.uk or find him on X @tomjs The boss of JP Morgan has met Andy Burnham and John Healey amid fears of a new windfall tax on banks. Jamie Dimon, who has led the Wall Street lender for more than 20 years, met the Prime Minister and Chancellor in London on Wednesday after a phone call with the latter last month. It comes just weeks before Mr Healey delivers his first Budget as Chancellor. He is under pressure to find billions of pounds to repair the public finances after the fallout from the Iran war derailed the Government’s plans. The American banker, who has met many chancellors during his period in charge of JP Morgan, was a strong supporter of Mr Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves. “They are smart and dedicated and they are working with business and collaborating, which is the only way to make things work,” he said of the former chancellor and Sir Keir Starmer in an interview with The Sunday Times. During Ms Reeves’s spell as chancellor, she resisted calls to raid lenders for more tax, calling financial services “the crown jewel in the UK economy” and instead encouraged regulators to relax rules in the City. However, there are concerns that Mr Healey may raise levies on banks in his Budget on Oct 28. Mr Burnham dropped into a meeting between Mr Dimon and Varun Chandra, the Prime Minister’s chief business adviser, according to the Financial Times. Mr Dimon has previously warned Andy Burnham against the idea. The JP Morgan boss said in an interview earlier this year that there would be “adverse consequences” if Labour targeted lenders with fresh windfall taxes. He said: “It would be one more negative on that bucket of things you got to think about. “I always thought it was wrong. We’re a great citizen [in the UK]. We hire people there. We want to be bigger there. We train people there. We hire veterans there.” The American banker added: “So if a government decides to do it, there’s nothing I can do, but it will over time cause decisions made that they may not like.” There have been growing calls from unions and campaigners to raise taxes on banks. Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, has argued that Mr Burnham could raise £9bn in four years simply by reversing the previous Conservative government’s cut to the bank surcharge. The group has argued that this could be used to fund cuts to energy bills. The Green Party also recently called for a 38pc windfall tax on banks to fund a tax cut for small businesses. Jane Fraser, the boss of Citi, another Wall Street bank, has warned that any increase in taxes risks making the UK a prohibitively expensive place to do business. She said during a visit to London last month that “money moves with its feet”, pointing out that “even Frankfurt and Paris are lower” when it comes to taxes for banks. Mr Healey said this week that “doubling down” on “more growth generated in more places” will be a central priority of his first Budget. He has refused to rule out raising taxes, but promised to “balance the books” and “control public spending”.

title: JP Morgan boss Jamie Dimon warns UK chancellor against bank tax hike - The Guardian
content: Wall Street CEO holds meeting with John Healey amid speculation over windfall tax on banks in October budget Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of the largest US bank, JP Morgan, is understood to have warned the UK chancellor, John Healey, against raising taxes on banks in his inaugural budget in October. The Wall Street billionaire met the new chancellor on Wednesday and cautioned him that higher taxes could put investment and employment in the UK at risk, it is understood. The meeting came amid speculation that Healey is considering a windfall tax on banks and oil companies in his budget on 28 October. Dimon has a long track record of lobbying against Britain’s additional bank taxes, which were imposed after the government bailed out big UK lenders in the 2008 financial crisis. Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, as well as a separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets. The JP Morgan chief executive has previously warned that raising these taxes further could have “adverse consequences”. In August, he told Healey in a telephone conversation that higher levies could hit jobs, citing a fall in finance roles in New York that he blamed on the city’s tax regime. Dimon was among a group of bank bosses who successfully lobbied against higher taxes before Healey’s predecessor Rachel Reeves’s budget last year – with Dimon hosting Varun Chandra, who remains in his post as the prime minister’s business envoy, at a birthday celebration for King Charles at the bank’s Manhattan headquarters. Days afterwards, Dimon announced plans to build a 3m sq ft tower in London’s Canary Wharf district, although he added that a “continuing positive business environment in the UK” was required. However, in May this year, he said he could scrap plans for the £3bn tower – which is expected to serve as JP Morgan’s UK headquarters and house more than half its 23,000-strong UK workforce – if Keir Starmer were replaced by a new Labour prime minister who was hostile to banks. However, he has faced calls to introduce higher levies from the TUC and the campaign group Positive Money, which argue a tax increase could help cover rising household bills as part of his drive to tackle the cost of living. The UK’s four biggest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds Banking Group – have generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years, largely off the back of rising interest rates. UK banks together paid an estimated £43.3bn in tax for the financial year that ended in March 2025, according to a report commissioned by the industry body UK Finance.

The boss of JP Morgan has met Andy Burnham and John Healey amid fears of a new windfall tax on banks. Jamie Dimon, who has led the Wall Street lender for more than 20 years, met the Prime Minister and Chancellor in London on Wednesday after a phone call with the latter last month. It comes just weeks before Mr Healey delivers his first Budget as Chancellor. He is under pressure to find billions of pounds to repair the public finances after the fallout from the Iran war derailed the Government's plans. The American banker, who has met many chancellors during his period in charge of JP Morgan, was a strong supporter of Mr Healey's predecessor, Rachel Reeves. "They are smart and dedicated and they are working with business and collaborating, which is the only way to make things work," he said of the former chancellor and Sir Keir Starmer in an interview with The Sunday Times. During Ms Reeves's spell as chancellor, she resisted calls to raid lenders for more tax, calling financial services "the crown jewel in the UK economy" and instead encouraged regulators to relax rules in the City. However, there are concerns that Mr Healey may raise levies on banks in his Budget on Oct 28. Mr Burnham dropped into a meeting between Mr Dimon and Varun Chandra, the Prime Minister's chief business adviser, according to the Financial Times. Mr Dimon has previously warned Andy Burnham against the idea. The JP Morgan boss said in an interview earlier this year that there would be "adverse consequences" if Labour targeted lenders with fresh windfall taxes. He said: "It would be one more negative on that bucket of things you got to think about. "I always thought it was wrong. We're a great citizen [in the UK]. We hire people there. We want to be bigger there. We train people there. We hire veterans there." The American banker added: "So if a government decides to do it, there's nothing I can do, but it will over time cause decisions made that they may not like." There have been growing calls from unions and campaigners to raise taxes on banks. title: JP Morgan names regional tech banking heads to international co-leadership roles - The American Bazaar
content: JPMorgan Chase & Co. has named its Asia-Pacific and EMEA technology investment banking heads as co-heads of international technology investment banking, according to an internal company memo seen Tuesday by Reuters and confirmed by a company spokesperson. The bank appointed Mark Fiteny, who serves as head of Asia-Pacific Technology, Media, and Telecom (APAC TMT) and New Economy Investment Banking, alongside Matt Gehl, head of EMEA Technology Investment Banking, to lead the international unit jointly. In their expanded capacity, Fiteny and Gehl will focus on supporting JPMorgan’s technology clients globally. Both executives bring more than two decades of industry experience to the international co-head positions. READ: JPMorgan posts record profit as dealmaking, trading surge (July 14, 2026) Prior to taking on this expanded international mandate, Fiteny spent significant time tracking cross-border commercial opportunities and equity capital trends across the region. Before joining JPMorgan, where he held managing director and senior leadership roles across consumer internet and new economy sectors, he worked as an engineer at Procter & Gamble. Gehl brings extensive regional technology coverage expertise to the role, having led JPMorgan’s EMEA Technology Investment Banking division out of London. READ: JPMorgan hires Sri Kosaraju as global investment banking chair (January 8, 2026) His recent focus has centered on tech sector market shifts, capital raising, and emerging growth areas across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, including speaking on investment banking developments at major European technology forums such as JPMorgan’s Tech Stars conference. Under the new operational structure, Gehl will remain based in London, while Fiteny is said to continue to operate out of Hong Kong. Alongside the international co-head designations, the financial institution made adjustments to its regional technology coverage leadership in Europe. The firm appointed Pieter Himpe as co-head of EMEA Technology Investment Banking, where he will serve alongside veteran banker Bill Hutchings. Himpe previously held the position of head of EMEA Internet and Tech Services within the bank’s technology investment banking division. Keerthi Ramesh is a writer with The American Bazaar. Financial institutions face persistent cyber threats, making sophisticated monitoring and detection systems essential. Greater use of artificial intelligence could help identify unusual activity, strengthen fraud prevention, and improve the institution's ability to respond to emerging risks. This technology exposure also creates an unusual connection between traditional banking and the broader technology economy. Rather than being viewed purely as a conventional  Financial Stock, JPMorgan Chase increasingly has characteristics associated with large-scale technology platforms because of its enormous data infrastructure, digital customer base, and technology spending. Digital finance is another area attracting attention. The possibility of a JPMorgan-backed stablecoin reflects the broader transformation taking place across payments and financial infrastructure. Stablecoins are designed to maintain a stable value while operating through digital networks. Their development could have implications for payments, settlement, liquidity management, and financial transactions. For JPMorgan Chase, participation in this area could strengthen its role in the evolving digital payments ecosystem. However, the long-term impact remains dependent on regulation, adoption, infrastructure development, and customer demand. The significance of the initiative therefore extends beyond a single digital asset project. It highlights how traditional financial institutions are adapting to changes in financial technology. The valuation debate cannot be separated from regulation. Large financial institutions operate under extensive capital, liquidity, risk-management, consumer-protection, and compliance requirements. Changes to capital surcharge rules could influence how much equity major banks need to maintain against their balance sheets. Higher capital requirements can strengthen resilience, but they can also affect returns and the amount of capital available for other corporate purposes. Regulatory discussions therefore remain an important part of the JPMorgan Chase outlook. The company has considerable scale and financial resources, which can help it navigate changing rules. Still, regulatory developments can influence profitability and valuation even when underlying customer demand remains healthy. Another consideration is the ongoing exposure that comes with operating a massive financial institution. Banks face legal, regulatory, compliance, and conduct-related risks across multiple business lines. Even when such issues do not materially alter the broader franchise, they can affect market sentiment and introduce uncertainty around future costs. This is especially relevant for a company trading at a valuation that already reflects considerable confidence in its earnings power. The stronger the expectations embedded in the share price, the more closely the market may monitor unexpected expenses, regulatory developments, and operational setbacks. Despite the valuation debate, the underlying franchise remains a major strength. JPMorgan Chase has a broad customer base, extensive financial infrastructure, strong brand recognition, and exposure to numerous areas of the economy. Its diversified business model also provides balance. Consumer banking can benefit from household financial activity, while commercial banking is linked to business demand. Investment banking and markets operations can benefit from capital-market activity, and asset management provides another recurring source of financial revenue. This diversification can help reduce reliance on a single economic driver. For a large financial institution, that breadth can become particularly valuable during periods when individual business lines experience different conditions. The Excess Returns approach is useful because it looks beyond simple market multiples. Instead of asking whether the stock trades at a high or low earnings multiple, the framework asks whether the company can generate returns above its required cost of equity. If JPMorgan Chase can continue producing returns that exceed that threshold, the business creates economic value over time. That supports the argument that the current market valuation may not fully capture the company's long-term earnings capability. However, valuation models are sensitive to assumptions. Future profitability, long-term growth, required returns, capital needs, and economic conditions can all change the resulting intrinsic value. The model therefore provides an analytical perspective rather than a guarantee about where the share price should trade. Several factors could reshape the valuation debate. Sustained earnings strength would reinforce the argument that the company's premium franchise deserves continued recognition. A slowdown in profitability could have the opposite effect, particularly if market expectations remain elevated. Interest-rate conditions will also matter because they influence lending economics, deposit behavior, credit quality, and market activity. Credit losses are another important consideration. A weakening economy could pressure borrowers and increase provisions, while a healthy economic environment could support loan activity and financial stability. Regulatory changes, capital requirements, technology spending, cybersecurity developments, and digital-payment adoption could also influence the longer-term narrative. JPMorgan Chase occupies an unusual position within the financial landscape. It combines the characteristics of a traditional bank with the scale and technology infrastructure of a modern financial platform. That combination makes its earnings story broader than conventional lending activity. At the same time, its size means that expectations are high. The market is likely to continue evaluating whether strong profitability can remain durable, whether technology investments translate into better efficiency, and whether emerging digital-finance initiatives create meaningful long-term value. The valuation debate will remain central because even a high-quality financial institution can face pressure when expectations become too demanding. The current JPMorgan Chase story is not simply about whether the business is performing well. The business clearly has significant strengths, including diversified operations, resilient earnings generation, substantial scale, and a powerful financial franchise. The bigger question is how much of that strength is already reflected in the share price. The Excess Returns framework offers a constructive argument by suggesting that continued economic value creation could support a higher intrinsic valuation. Meanwhile, conventional market comparisons suggest that the shares are not obviously discounted relative to peers. That creates a fascinating divide between fundamental quality and valuation comfort. JPMorgan Chase remains one of the most closely watched names in the financial sector because its earnings strength, technological ambitions, digital-finance strategy, and regulatory exposure are all converging at an important point for the valuation story. The company has demonstrated an ability to generate strong returns on equity, while its investments in AI and digital infrastructure could support longer-term efficiency and competitiveness. Yet the share price has already enjoyed a powerful run, making future earnings execution increasingly important. The central issue is therefore straightforward: can JPMorgan Chase continue delivering enough earnings power and economic value to justify the expectations embedded in its current valuation? That question could keep the stock firmly on the market radar as the financial sector moves through its next phase. Discover our approach, digital tools and community initiatives. A donor-advised fund can help you support students’ education in a way that reflects your values and honors your legacy. Executive Director, Family Engagement and Governance If education changed your life – or you’ve seen financial barriers hold others back – you might want to consider a donor-advised fund (DAF), which can be a flexible, organized giving engine to expand access through a focused education strategy. With a single contribution, you can establish a dedicated giving vehicle, recommend grants and support students in a way that both reflects your values and honors your family’s legacy. When paired with a thoughtfully designed scholarship program, a DAF allows you to move from writing checks to building a durable platform for talent, access and upward mobility. “Many clients want to support education for underprivileged children and young adults, but often experience analysis/paralysis, and feel overwhelmed about where to give,” said Brad Fine, wealth advisor with the Hamline Fine Group, J.P. Morgan Wealth Management. “A DAF is a great first step. Clients can contribute now – partner with our team on refining a giving strategy – and recommend grants as they see fit.” Scholarships are uniquely powerful because they operate at the intersection of aspiration and constraint: Indeed, a capable student’s academic trajectory can hinge on a gap in tuition, books, housing or unpaid internship costs. Using a DAF to fund scholarships lets you focus your philanthropy on real outcomes – who is helped, how selection aligns with your personal mission and what success looks like – while leveraging experienced partners to handle eligibility rules, application workflows, award disbursement and compliance. The result is often a program that is more scalable and less administratively burdensome than a bespoke approach, without sacrificing the personal touch that makes scholarship giving so meaningful. Whether your goal is to expand access for first-generation students, strengthen a profession you’ve built your career in or invest in a community that shaped you, a DAF-backed scholarship strategy can be structured to endure across market cycles and generations. With these key design choices, governance considerations and practical steps in mind, you can help ensure your scholarship philanthropy is impactful, compliant and built to last. Typically, you can’t use your DAF to give scholarships directly to students. Most DAF sponsors, including National Philanthropic Trust, do not allow grants that go directly to individuals (including students) because it can be seen as intentionally benefiting someone and raise regulatory concerns. Instead, the typical approach is to grant to a qualified public charity – often a school, university foundation or scholarship-administering nonprofit – that then awards scholarships through its own process. The charity must retain full discretion and control over scholarship selection and payments. While you can often provide nonbinding input – such as scholarship purpose, general criteria and populations served – you typically cannot: You can usually name the scholarship after yourself, your family or someone else (e.g., the “Smith Family Scholarship”), as long as the arrangement doesn’t provide more than incidental benefits. If you have strong ties to your alma mater, you can often use your DAF to fund scholarships there, if you grant to the institution or to its 501(c)(3) foundation and the institution controls the scholarship program. “The flexibility of a DAF allowed our client to make a large year-end gift for tax planning and later work with his alma mater to launch a named scholarship,” said Steve Soja, wealth partner of Soja West Group at J.P. Morgan Wealth Management. You can even use your DAF to pay tuition at a private K–12 school, but this arrangement can be more complicated. In fact, many DAF sponsors restrict K–12 tuition assistance because of heightened concern for potential private benefit. If this use is allowed, the scholarship program must be structured and administered by a qualified charity with clear, charitable selection criteria and independence. While you’ll have some leeway when it comes to building your scholarship, there are some limitations to bear in mind. You can often use geographic or community-based criteria (e.g., hometown, county, specific school district). You can also require objective, charitable criteria, such as financial need, demonstrated academic interest, intended field of study, first-generation or underrepresented status, record of community service, specific grade point average and so on. Criteria that are overly narrow or designed to benefit a preselected person or class can be problematic. You can’t use DAF grants to confer a private benefit on disqualified persons – including yourself, family members and controlled entities – or to steer funds to friends or associates. Most sponsors will prohibit any arrangement that could benefit a donor’s family. Nor can you use DAF funds to pay for tickets, event tables or admissions, or for sponsorships that provide a more-than-incidental benefit. If you attend an event, pay the personal portion separately (and consult your sponsor on the rules). DAF scholarship money can cover travel, laptops or living expenses only if the charity’s scholarship policy treats these as qualified educational expenses and administers them properly. The charity – not the donor – decides what expenses are covered and how payments are made. You can also support mentoring programs, but you’ll have to avoid arrangements that suggest the scholarship is tied to employment, guaranteed internships or benefits to your business. If you want your scholarship to have an internship component, the charity should design it independently and make the opportunity broadly available. To ensure the scholarship stays aligned with your goals, or “donor intent,” you can often specify the following: You generally cannot, however, impose restrictions that remove the charity’s discretion or create an enforceable personal benefit. Given education privacy laws, many charities can provide only aggregate reporting, such as number of awards, total dollars, school distribution and impact narratives. They can’t share personally identifying student information without consent. A DAF can be a powerful way to support education - especially when it’s paired with a scholarship program run by a qualified public charity. Because DAFs generally can’t make grants directly to individuals, the most durable approach is to fund an independent scholarship process where the charity retains full discretion over selection and payments. With clear, charitable criteria and the right governance guardrails, you can translate your giving goals into meaningful student outcomes all while keeping the program scalable, compliant and built to last. title: JP Morgan downgrades Bytes over AI lag as Computacenter leads pack - Yahoo Finance UK
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results Bytes Technology Group PLC (LSE:BYIT, FRA:9NY, JSE:BYI) received a less favourable call from JP Morgan on Monday, as the bank initiated coverage with an 'underweight' rating and named peer Computacenter PLC (LSE:CCC) its top pick in the European value-added reseller (VAR) sector. Shares in Bytes tumbled 2% to 414.40 on Monday, while Computacenter ticked higher to 5,615p, moves that came as JP Morgan set its 'underweight' rating on Bytes and reiterated an 'overweight (OW)' stance on Computacenter. Diving into the rationale, the note said JPMorgan preferred VARs with stronger exposure to AI monetisation, particularly those more geared toward hyperscale capital expenditure. On that basis, Computacenter was identified as its most preferred name in the subsector. Turning to the downgrade, JP Morgan said Bytes had relatively limited tangible AI exposure, with hardware accounting for less than 10% of its gross profit. Broadening the scope, the broker said its VAR note addressed investor questions on AI monetisation, the threat of disintermediation, changes to vendor incentives and related topics. JP Morgan said those limited hardware and AI exposures, plus recent changes in vendor incentives, create risk to consensus earnings estimates for Bytes. Looking beyond immediate forecasts, the note also considered the risk of vendor disintermediation in the subsector, a theme that could pressure intermediaries that struggle to demonstrate strategic value. Now They Almost Agree — Near $4,500 Published: 04-17-2026, 02:51 pm | Updated: 09-07-2026, 02:15 pm As of September 2026, major bank gold price forecasts for year-end 2026 have converged lower. J.P. Morgan is at $4,500. Wells Fargo is at $4,900-$5,100. Goldman Sachs is at $4,900, and UBS is at $5,500. Bank of America’s average estimate sits near $4,360. Gold trades near $4,436, about 21% below its January 28, 2026 all-time high of $5,589.38. Bank forecasts and price data last verified September 2026. Every bank figure below carries its own as-of date. Forecasts here have moved twice since our last update. This table will keep moving. Gold is trading around $4,190/oz — approximately 25% below its all-time high of $5,589.38, set on January 28, 2026 [Trading Economics; CBS News]. The major bank consensus for year-end 2026 now ranges from $4,900 (Goldman Sachs) to $6,300 (J.P. Morgan and Wells Fargo) [Goldman Sachs; J.P. Morgan Global Research; Wells Fargo Investment Institute]. Most analysts remain directionally bullish, though Goldman Sachs and UBS have revised their targets lower as Fed rate-cut expectations shifted into 2027. This gold price analysis 2026–2027 covers every major bank’s current forecast, the five forces driving them, and the risks that could derail the rally. Gold gained around 65% in 2025 — its strongest annual performance since 1979 — setting 53 new all-time highs along the way [World Gold Council, Gold Demand Trends Full Year 2025; LBMA Gold Price Data]. In January 2026, spot gold pierced $5,000 for the first time in history before peaking at $5,589.38 on January 28 [CBS News]. Then came March. Gold fell more than 10% — its sharpest monthly decline since June 2013 — as the US-Iran conflict pushed oil prices higher, raised inflation expectations, and strengthened the dollar [World Gold Council, Gold Market Commentary, March 2026]. As of September 2026, gold is trading near $4,436, having recovered above the $4,400–$4,600 support zone several institutions flagged as structurally significant. This is not structural retreat. It is consolidation after an extraordinary run — and most institutions are treating it accordingly. Official sector buyers purchased 863.3 tonnes of gold in 2025 — more than double the 2010–2021 annual average of 473 tonnes [World Gold Council, Gold Demand Trends Full Year 2025]. The World Gold Council’s central bank survey found 95% of respondents expect global gold reserves to increase over the next 12 months, with a record 43% planning to expand their own holdings and none anticipating a reduction [World Gold Council, Central Bank Gold Reserves Survey 2025]. J.P. Morgan projects central banks will purchase around 800 tonnes in 2026 [J.P. Morgan Global Research, February 2026]. Emerging market central banks — led by China, Poland, India, and Turkey — are systematically replacing dollar-denominated reserves with gold. China’s central bank extended its accumulation streak to 15 consecutive months through January 2026 [World Gold Council, China Gold Market Update, February 2026]. The 2022 freezing of Russian dollar reserves accelerated a strategic shift that has only deepened since. Markets are pricing in further cuts in 2026. Goldman Sachs estimates that every 50 basis points of Fed easing adds approximately $120 per ounce of price support for gold — by reducing the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset and weakening the dollar [Goldman Sachs via TheWealthAdvisor]. Western gold ETFs added roughly 500 tonnes since the start of 2025, running well ahead of what rate cuts alone explain [Goldman Sachs via TheStreet]. Global gold ETF inflows reached a record $89 billion in 2025, pushing total holdings to an all-time high of 4,025 tonnes [World Gold Council, ETF Holdings and Flows, December 2025]. Rising sovereign debt and eroding confidence in fiat monetary systems are driving physical bar purchases and institutional call-option buying. Goldman Sachs calls this the “debasement trade” and identifies it as one of the three core pillars of its bullish thesis [Goldman Sachs via TheWealthAdvisor]. Here is a clean comparison of each major bank’s gold price per ounce forecast for year-end 2026, with the reasoning behind each call. J.P. Morgan cut its Q4 2026 gold target by 25% on July 3, 2026. The new target is $4,500, down from $6,000 just weeks earlier, on June 9. The bank now projects a Q3 2026 average of $4,300. The driver is rate sensitivity. J.P. Morgan estimates gold moves roughly $20/oz for every 1 basis point rise in 10-year real yields since late February. The bank’s long-term thesis is unchanged, though. It still expects a renewed upward cycle in 2027, driven by central bank diversification and real-yield normalization. J.P. Morgan is now the most cautious major bank on a 2026 year-end basis. Wells Fargo Investment Institute has cut its 2026 gold target twice since February. It had raised the target to $6,100-$6,300 that month. The current range is $4,900-$5,100, down from $5,300-$5,500 previously. Its 2027 target fell too, to $5,400-$5,600 from $5,800-$6,000. The bank calls this a recalibration, not a reversal. The new range still implies 11-16% upside from current levels. Two February assumptions didn’t hold: the Fed did not cut as expected, and central bank buying slowed. UBS has moved away from a single year-end number and now publishes a quarterly path. As of August 2026, that path runs $4,400 by September 2026, $4,600 by December 2026, $5,000 by March 2027, and $5,200 by June 2027. The bank extended the horizon further that same month, adding a $5,400 target by end-September 2027. UBS estimates gold needs roughly 500 tonnes of quarterly investment demand to hold $5,000 or better, and still expects annual central bank buying in the 750–1,000 tonne range. The bank treats pullbacks toward $4,000 as a buying opportunity rather than a reversal signal. Bank of America cut its 2026 average gold forecast by 14% on July 8, 2026. The new figure is $4,360, down from $6,000, citing a more hawkish Federal Reserve outlook. That earlier $6,000 figure was a 12-month target set before the cut. It is no longer current. BofA still sees $5,000 within reach once the Fed’s tightening cycle ends. Analyst Michael Widmer points to structural fiscal deficits and low investor gold allocations as underappreciated long-term supports. Goldman Sachs cut its year-end 2026 target from $5,400 to $4,900 on June 20, 2026, a $500 reduction that analysts Daan Struyven and Lina Thomas attributed to two converging pressures: fading gold ETF inflows (including the first monthly Asian ETF outflow since August 2025) and the removal of all remaining 2026 rate cuts from Goldman’s forecast, with easing now delayed to June and December 2027 [Goldman Sachs Global Research; TheStreet, June 20, 2026]. The cut follows a sequence: Goldman raised its target from $4,900 to $5,400 in January, held that call through March’s sharp correction, then revised it lower once ETF demand softened materially. The structural framework — central bank buying, de-dollarisation, the debasement trade — remains the long-term basis; Goldman still describes the medium-term risk as skewed to the upside. The revision is also the clearest measure of how much the bullish thesis was rate-dependent. Goldman’s new base case strips out Fed easing entirely and still lands at $4,900 — meaning a $500 haircut from when cuts were in the model. The long-duration structural buyers remain. The near-term investor demand that amplified the bull run has stepped back. Morgan Stanley revised its H2 target from $5,700 down to $5,200 by Q4 2026, citing elevated real yields and delayed Fed cuts [Morgan Stanley Commodities Research, April 2026]. It remains the most measured call on this list, but the direction is still higher — and $5,200 represents roughly 24% upside from current levels. The bank sees momentum from 2025 fading, but the broader trend remaining higher. Commerzbank raised its year-end forecast from $4,400 to $5,000 [Reuters analyst forecast compilation]. It shares the structural bull thesis but tempers it with valuation concern. Its 2027 target is $5,200. HSBC is the lone dissenter. Analyst James Steel maintains a wide 2026 trading range rather than a point target [TheStreet], arguing that any meaningful easing of geopolitical tensions or fiscal tightening could remove a significant portion of the current risk premium. It is the only major bank on this list with a credible downside scenario. The gold price forecast for 2027 is broadly bullish across virtually every institution, though the range of targets widens considerably — two years of compounding uncertainty will do that. J.P. Morgan expects gold to average $5,400/oz by Q4 2027 [J.P. Morgan Global Research]. Goldman Sachs also targets $5,400 for 2027, citing continued central bank accumulation and normalizing ETF inflows at higher price levels [Bloomberg; ExchangeRates.org.uk]. Commerzbank’s 2027 target is $5,200 [Reuters analyst forecast compilation]. Bank of America has flagged that in an extreme demand scenario — accelerated de-dollarization, further Fed easing, and rising institutional gold allocations — prices could reach $8,000 by 2027 [Bank of America via TheStreet]. That is the bull case, not the base case. But none of the conditions required are implausible. The case that $4,500 has become a floor, not just a support level, comes down to who is buying. Central banks are now the dominant marginal buyers of gold. They don’t sell on bad days — which means the old relationship between corrections and structural demand has fundamentally changed. Any long-term gold price forecast that ignores this structural shift in who holds the marginal bid is working from an outdated model. For a broader view of how this demand shift is reshaping the entire complex, our long-term silver forecasts explore the same structural forces at work in silver. A complete gold investment outlook for 2026 requires an honest accounting of what could push prices lower. Four scenarios could put the rally in reverse. A hawkish Fed pivot: If inflation reaccelerates and forces the Fed to pause or reverse rate cuts, real yields rise and the dollar strengthens. Both are direct headwinds for gold. A sustained dollar rally: Dollar strength is the single most reliable short-term headwind for gold. Wells Fargo explicitly flags stronger-than-expected US economic performance in H2 2026 as a risk to its own bullish call [Wells Fargo Investment Institute]. Geopolitical risk resolution: A credible easing of the US-Iran conflict, or a serious US fiscal consolidation plan, could deflate the fear premium embedded in current prices. HSBC has been the most explicit about this scenario [HSBC via TheStreet]. Speculative unwind. The 2025 rally attracted speculative positioning on top of structural demand. When that unwinds, it moves fast — as March demonstrated. The correction was painful; it was also, for most structural buyers, irrelevant. Goldman Sachs made the key point after March: the institutions that drove gold higher — central banks and long-duration allocators — were not the ones selling [Goldman Sachs via TheStreet]. They are still accumulating. Gold is approximately 25% below its January all-time high [Trading Economics]. Wells Fargo told clients to buy the dip [Wells Fargo Investment Institute via TheStreet]. J.P. Morgan identifies $4,400–$4,600 as a strong support zone, with 35–45% upside to its year-end target from those levels [J.P. Morgan Global Research]. Goldman Sachs held its $5,400 target through the March correction before revising to $4,900 in late June as ETF inflows softened — a call that still implies 17% upside from current levels [Goldman Sachs Global Research; TheStreet]. Gold has gained roughly 360% since 2015. Every meaningful correction across that decade — 2018, 2020, 2022 — resolved as a consolidation within the uptrend. Understanding gold price trends across 2026–2027 requires that historical context: the underlying case today is stronger than at any prior point in that cycle — central banks buying at more than double the pre-2022 pace, record ETF holdings of 4,025 tonnes [World Gold Council], and a de-dollarisation trend measured in decades. Gold’s function has also shifted. It is no longer simply a crisis hedge — it now serves as a debasement hedge, a dollar diversifier, and a reserve asset for institutions quietly reassessing the long-term safety of fiat systems. That wider role supports a higher structural price floor than the old safe-haven framework ever did. The same structural forces are playing out across the broader precious metals complex — our silver price trends analysis covers how silver fits into this cycle for investors thinking beyond gold alone. For a longer view on where gold itself may be headed, our gold price predictions overview puts the current cycle in fuller historical context. Gold is 13% off its all-time high. The structural case that drove it there has not changed. Central banks are buying at more than double their pre-2022 pace. Meanwhile, ETF inflows in 2025 hit a record $89 billion [World Gold Council, ETF Holdings and Flows, December 2025]. On top of that, the debasement concern — rising sovereign debt, eroding confidence in fiat systems — is, if anything, intensifying rather than fading. The year-end 2026 consensus now sits between $4,900 (Goldman Sachs) and ~$6,000 (J.P. Morgan), with Wells Fargo at $6,100–$6,300, Bank of America at $6,000, UBS at $5,500, and Morgan Stanley at $5,200. Goldman Sachs and UBS revised their targets lower in May–June as rate-cut expectations pushed into 2027 and ETF inflows softened — adjusting the timing of the rally, not the direction [Goldman Sachs; J.P. Morgan Global Research; Wells Fargo Investment Institute; UBS]. For 2027, J.P. Morgan targets $6,300 by year-end and Goldman Sachs points to $5,400, with Bank of America’s bull case reaching $8,000 [J.P. Morgan Global Research; Bloomberg; Bank of America via TheStreet]. The structural case — central bank buying, de-dollarisation, debasement concern — is what the major institutions are holding onto. The near-term rate-sensitive demand has stepped back. That gap is where H2 2026 plays out. Whether you’re building a position for the first time or adding to an existing one, having a clear view of gold price predictions for 2026 matters. Beyond the headline numbers, understanding the structural forces behind them — rising sovereign debt, central bank demand, and fiat erosion — is equally important. Ultimately, both factors matter as much as the price you pay. Learn more about owning gold and silver at GoldSilver.com. Get important market alerts sent straight to your inbox. As of late June 2026, the major bank consensus places gold between $4,900 (Goldman Sachs, revised June 20) and ~$6,000 (J.P. Morgan) by year-end, with Wells Fargo at $6,100–$6,300, Bank of America at $6,000, UBS at $5,500, and Morgan Stanley at $5,200. Gold is currently trading near $4,190 — approximately 25% below its January 2026 all-time high of $5,589 — meaning every major bank forecast implies significant upside from current levels. Goldman Sachs’ model implies $6,350/oz if central bank and ETF flows hit maximum assumptions [Goldman Sachs]. Five: central bank accumulation projected at around 800 tonnes in 2026 [J.P. Morgan Global Research]; de-dollarization by emerging-market reserve managers; Federal Reserve rate cuts reducing the opportunity cost of holding gold; record ETF inflows of $89 billion in 2025 [World Gold Council]; and the “debasement trade” — institutional concern about the long-term credibility of sovereign debt and fiat currencies [Goldman Sachs]. Most major banks say yes. Goldman Sachs — the most conservative — forecasts $5,400/oz [Goldman Sachs]. J.P. Morgan, Wells Fargo, UBS, and Bank of America all forecast above $6,000. Gold already traded above $5,000 in January 2026. The live debate among analysts is no longer about whether gold returns there — instead, the real question is whether it ultimately reaches $6,000 or beyond. At the start of 2025, institutional consensus clustered around $2,800–$3,200. By April 2026, those same institutions are forecasting $5,400–$6,300 [J.P. Morgan Global Research; Goldman Sachs; Wells Fargo Investment Institute]. That is not price-chasing.
